prompt: Three of the four engines in this lesson are one kind of thing and the fourth is another. What is the split?
hint: It is about where the database code runs, not about how much data it holds.

choices.text: Three are free to use; SQLite needs a commercial licence
choices.why: SQLite is public domain, and it is the freest of the four.

choices.text: Three handle large databases; SQLite handles small ones
choices.why: Size is not the line. SQLite handles a database larger than most companies have.

choices.text: Three are servers; SQLite is a library in your process
choices.why: A server listens on a socket and has its own process. SQLite is linked into yours and the database is a file.

choices.text: Three are relational; SQLite stores key-value pairs
choices.why: SQLite is fully relational and fully transactional, with foreign keys, CHECK and window functions.

prompt: A colleague says MariaDB is "just a rebranded MySQL". What is wrong with that?
hint: Think about who forked what, and when, and how long ago that was.

choices.text: A 2009 fork, developed separately since: mostly agreed, not entirely
choices.why: Same ancestor, same protocol, same client; fifteen years of separate work have produced real differences.

choices.text: MariaDB was written from scratch and shares no code with MySQL
choices.why: It is a fork of MySQL's code, which is why the protocol, the client and most of the dialect are shared.

choices.text: MySQL is the fork, and MariaDB is the original it was taken from
choices.why: The other way round. MySQL is the original; MariaDB is the fork the authors started when Oracle acquired Sun.

choices.text: They are the same codebase under two names, released by one team
choices.why: Different teams, different releases, different licences for the engine.

prompt: Match each engine to the thing this lesson says is most characteristic of it.
hint: One is about who owns it, one about how it is deployed, one about what it refuses.

pairs.right: the strictest, with an extension mechanism
owned by Oracle, an enormous installed base
the 2009 fork, GPL with no commercial edition
a library, not a server, and a database in one file

right_distractors: a key-value store with an SQL layer

prompt: Which of the four is in the public domain?
hint: It is also the one deployed on every phone.

choices.text: SQLite
choices.why: Public domain, which is part of why it can be embedded in anything at all.

choices.text: PostgreSQL
choices.why: It has a permissive licence of its own, which is not the same as public domain.

choices.text: MariaDB
choices.why: GPL, with no commercial edition of the engine behind it.

choices.text: MySQL
choices.why: Dual-licensed: GPL for the community edition, commercial for the rest.

prompt: A team is picking a database for a service that several application servers will write to, and one argument raised is that PostGIS would be useful later. Which engine does that second point rule out?
hint: PostGIS is not a product; it is something loaded into a particular engine.

choices.text: MySQL, which has no way to store geographic data
choices.why: MySQL has spatial types. The point about PostGIS is where it runs, not that nothing else has geography.

choices.text: Everything but PostgreSQL: PostGIS is an extension of it
choices.why: PostGIS is Postgres with something loaded into it, and the extension mechanism is the thing the other three do not have.

choices.text: SQLite, which was already ruled out by the several writers
choices.why: True about SQLite, but the several writers ruled it out already; the question asks what the second point adds.

choices.text: Neither point rules anything out: PostGIS runs alongside an engine
choices.why: It is not a separate server. It is an extension loaded into PostgreSQL.

prompt: The same three-table report was sent to PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite. What came back?
hint: Look at what was in the rows, and separately at what drew the boxes around them.

choices.text: The same rows, drawn differently by each client
choices.why: The rules and boxes are the clients' formatting. The rows are the database's answer, and they agreed.

choices.text: Three different row orders, because ORDER BY is engine-specific
choices.why: ORDER BY means the same thing on all four; the sort was identical.

choices.text: The query failed on two of them and needed rewriting
choices.why: It ran unchanged. Joins, GROUP BY and ORDER BY are shared ground.

choices.text: Identical output, byte for byte, from the three engines
choices.why: The rows matched; the frames did not, and one revenue column differed in its decimals.

prompt: Somebody finds a 2015 article saying window functions are a PostgreSQL feature the other engines lack. What should you check before believing it?
hint: The lesson dates the arrival of window functions on each engine for exactly this reason.

choices.text: Whether the version in front of you is that old
choices.why: The claim was true when written and is false on anything installed today; the version is what decides.

choices.text: There is no need: window functions remain a PostgreSQL feature
choices.why: MySQL 8.0 and SQLite 3.25 both arrived in 2018, and MariaDB 10.2 in 2017.

choices.text: Whether the query uses OVER, since that is the PostgreSQL spelling
choices.why: OVER is the standard spelling on all four.

choices.text: Whether the table is large enough for the engine to allow them
choices.why: Nothing about window functions depends on table size.

prompt: The differences fall into four groups: what the engine refuses, how ___ is compared, the dialect, and how it is run.
hint: One word, and the section on it is about collation.

prompt: Which of these is NOT a difference between the four engines?
hint: Three of these are engine behaviour and one is not an engine feature at all.

choices.text: Whether an ambiguous GROUP BY is refused
choices.why: That is a real difference: PostgreSQL and MySQL refuse it, MariaDB and SQLite do not.

choices.text: Whether text comparison ignores case by default
choices.why: A real difference, and the one behind a UNIQUE that does not mean what you think.

choices.text: What a primary key and a foreign key mean
choices.why: The relational model is not an engine feature. Keys mean the same thing on all four and on the fifth.

choices.text: Whether ALTER TABLE can be rolled back
choices.why: A real difference: PostgreSQL and SQLite put DDL in the transaction, MySQL and MariaDB commit it.

prompt: A report written and tested on PostgreSQL is moved to SQLite and the totals come out slightly different, though every row matches. Where would you look first?
hint: The report sums a money column, and the two engines do not hold that column the same way.

choices.text: The JOIN, which is pairing the rows differently here
choices.why: The row counts matched, so the join produced the same pairs.

choices.text: The ORDER BY, which is not stable across engines
choices.why: An unstable sort reorders rows; it does not change a sum.

choices.text: How the money column is stored on SQLite
choices.why: NUMERIC(10,2) is an affinity there; the values went through floating point and the sum inherits it.

choices.text: The GROUP BY, which groups NULL differently on SQLite
choices.why: Both group NULL as one group, and the row counts already showed the grouping agreed.

prompt: What does SQLite have instead of a connection over a socket?
hint: The library is inside your program.

choices.text: A named pipe to a helper process
choices.why: There is no second process at all; that is the whole point.

choices.text: A socket on a port the library picks for you
choices.why: No port, no listener, nothing to connect to.

choices.text: A function call in your own process
choices.why: The library is linked into your program, so there is no process boundary to cross.

choices.text: An HTTP call to a local service
choices.why: Nothing is served. The database is a file the library reads.

prompt: A second process tried to write while the first held a transaction open, and got `database is locked`. What is the scope of that lock?
hint: Not the row, and not the table.

choices.text: The whole database file
choices.why: One writer per database, whatever it is writing. That is the single cost of having no server.

choices.text: The row being updated
choices.why: SQLite does not lock at the row level; the two statements touched different rows and it still failed.

choices.text: The table being written to
choices.why: Not the table either. The two statements were both on `products`, but a write to any table would have failed the same way.

choices.text: The connection, which had not been closed
choices.why: The second process had its own connection; what it met was the first one's write lock on the file.

prompt: What does turning on WAL mode fix, and what does it leave alone?
hint: Count the readers and count the writers.

choices.text: It allows several writers, and leaves reads unchanged
choices.why: The other way round. It is readers that stop contending; the writer count stays at one.

choices.text: It makes writes durable, which they were not before it
choices.why: SQLite is crash-safe in either journal mode; WAL changes how, not whether.

choices.text: It lets the file live on a network filesystem
choices.why: A network filesystem is not supported in either mode, because the file locks it needs are unreliable there.

choices.text: Readers stop contending; there is still one writer
choices.why: Most of the contention goes; the limit does not, and a queue in front of one writer is still one writer.

prompt: A 40 GB read-heavy catalogue serves one application process on one machine, with a nightly bulk load. A colleague says it is far too big for SQLite. What is the best answer?
hint: The lesson says which question actually rules SQLite out, and it is not this one.

choices.text: Agree: 40 GB is past what a single file can hold
choices.why: A SQLite database can be far larger than that; size is not the limit people think it is.

choices.text: Disagree: a single writer on one host is the shape it fits
choices.why: The question that rules it out is how many machines write, and here the answer is one.

choices.text: Agree: a read-heavy workload of that size needs a server's cache
choices.why: Reads do not contend, and there is no round trip; read-heavy on one machine is where SQLite does well.

choices.text: Disagree, provided the nightly load runs inside a transaction
choices.why: A transaction is good practice and is not what decides it; one writer on one machine already fits.

prompt: Which of these rules SQLite out of a deployment, whatever you tune?
hint: One of these is a fact about the architecture, not about load.

choices.text: A database that grows past a few gigabytes
choices.why: Size is not the limit; SQLite handles far more than that.

choices.text: Needing foreign keys and CHECK constraints enforced
choices.why: It has both, though foreign keys must be switched on per connection.

choices.text: Three application servers, all writing
choices.why: The file has to be local, and locking over a network filesystem is not supported. No tuning changes it.

choices.text: A few hundred writes a minute from one process
choices.why: One process writing is the shape it is built for; WAL and a busy timeout absorb this comfortably.

prompt: The backup of a live SQLite database is not `cp`. It is `sqlite3 shop.db ".___ out.db"`, or the equivalent API.
hint: The dot command says what it does.

prompt: `INSERT INTO order_lines VALUES (5, 2, 'three', 189.00)` was sent to all three. `quantity` is `INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0)`. What happened?
hint: Two engines named the column in an error; one did not.

choices.text: PostgreSQL and MySQL refused; SQLite stored it
choices.why: SQLite's declared type is an affinity, so a value it cannot convert is kept as it arrived.

choices.text: Each of the three refused it, with a different message
choices.why: SQLite stored it. The row holds the string `three` in an INTEGER column.

choices.text: Each of the three stored it, coercing it to zero
choices.why: Coercing to zero is what MySQL did before 5.7; today it refuses, and PostgreSQL always did.

choices.text: SQLite refused it and the other two coerced it
choices.why: Exactly backwards, which is the point of running it rather than arguing about it.

prompt: The string `three` went into `quantity`, and `CHECK (quantity > 0)` did not stop it. Why not?
hint: The CHECK ran. Ask what it compared.

choices.text: In SQLite text compares as greater than any number
choices.why: The type ordering puts text above numbers, so the constraint passed on a value that is not a quantity at all.

choices.text: CHECK constraints are not enforced by SQLite
choices.why: They are enforced. This one ran and returned true.

choices.text: The CHECK applies to values the column's type accepted
choices.why: There is no such rule; the constraint was evaluated on the value that was stored.

choices.text: NOT NULL replaces CHECK when both are on one column
choices.why: It does not replace it. Both were declared, both ran, and it is the CHECK that returned true.

prompt: `typeof(price)` on four rows of one `NUMERIC(10,2)` column came back `real`, `integer`, `integer`, `real`. What does that show?
hint: Four rows, one column, two answers.

choices.text: The column was declared with the wrong type
choices.why: It was declared exactly as lesson 3 asked. The declaration is an affinity rather than a rule.

choices.text: SQLite decides the storage type per value, not per column
choices.why: Dynamic typing: the value carries its type, and `1499.00` fits an integer while `349.90` does not.

choices.text: The rows were inserted by different clients
choices.why: One statement inserted all four.

choices.text: `typeof()` reports the declared type, and the declaration varies by row
choices.why: A declaration is per column. `typeof()` reports what is actually stored.

prompt: You are starting a new SQLite database for an application that holds prices. What two things does the lesson tell you to do?
hint: One is a keyword on the table; one is about the unit you store money in.

choices.text: Declare the tables STRICT, and keep money in cents
choices.why: STRICT enforces the declared type; cents avoid a float, because there is no decimal type to reach for.

choices.text: Declare the columns NUMERIC(10,2), and round on the way out
choices.why: NUMERIC is an affinity here. Rounding a float on the way out does not undo the arithmetic done on it.

choices.text: Turn on WAL mode, and add a CHECK that the price is positive
choices.why: Both are good and neither addresses the type. The CHECK passed on the string `three`.

choices.text: Store prices as TEXT, and cast them back at each read
choices.why: Casting in every query is a rule somebody forgets once; cents in an integer needs no discipline.

prompt: `SELECT city, name, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY city` returned Recife with `Ana Ribeiro` and a count of 2. Recife has two customers. What is the defect this illustrates?
hint: Ask what happened to the second customer, and what a reader of that report would conclude.

choices.text: The count is wrong, because it should be 1 for each name shown
choices.why: The count is right: two customers in Recife. It is the name beside it that is not a fact about the group.

choices.text: NULL cities were folded in with the named ones
choices.why: NULL got its own row in the output, which is correct and separate from this.

choices.text: The engine sorted by name instead of city
choices.why: The output is grouped by city; the sort is not what produced the missing customer.

choices.text: A value was taken from one arbitrary row, silently
choices.why: Nothing says which row. Carla Meneses is absent from a table with no gap in it, and no error was raised.

prompt: You have just been given access to an inherited MySQL server. Which single query tells you most about how strict it will be?
hint: One variable carries several of the refusals this section is about.

choices.text: `SELECT VERSION()`
choices.why: Useful, and it tells you what is available rather than what is switched on.

choices.text: `SHOW TABLES`
choices.why: It tells you what is there, not how the engine will behave when you write to it.

choices.text: `SELECT @@collation_database`
choices.why: Worth asking, and it answers the next section's question rather than this one's.

choices.text: `SELECT @@sql_mode`
choices.why: It names STRICT_TRANS_TABLES and ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, which are two of the three columns in the ranking table.

prompt: `WHERE email = 'ANA@EXAMPLE.COM'` found Ana on MySQL and nothing on PostgreSQL or SQLite. What is the reason?
hint: Something about the column decides how two strings are compared.

choices.text: MySQL lowercases a string on the way into storage
choices.why: The stored value was unchanged; it is the comparison rule that folds case, not the storage.

choices.text: The UNIQUE index on email makes the lookup case-insensitive
choices.why: The index follows the collation rather than setting it; a non-unique column behaves the same way.

choices.text: MySQL's default collation ignores case; the others' do not
choices.why: `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` folds case and accent, and it applies to every comparison the engine makes.

choices.text: PostgreSQL requires the address to be quoted differently
choices.why: The quoting was identical. What differed was the comparison rule.

prompt: In the collation name `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`, the suffix `ci` stands for case-___.
hint: And `ai` beside it is accent-insensitive.

prompt: An application stores API keys in `VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE` on MySQL with the default collation. What has quietly gone wrong?
hint: Two keys that differ only in case are the same value to that collation.

choices.text: Nothing; UNIQUE still refuses a duplicate key
choices.why: It refuses more than a duplicate: it refuses a genuinely different key that differs only in case.

choices.text: The column is too short for a key and silently truncates
choices.why: Truncation is a strict-mode question and is not what the collation does.

choices.text: UNIQUE does not apply to a VARCHAR column on MySQL
choices.why: It applies. The problem is what it considers equal.

choices.text: Keys differing only in case collide, and compare equal
choices.why: A key is not natural-language text. The default folds case, so `AbC…` and `abc…` are one value for both the index and the comparison.

prompt: Match each engine to the way the lesson gets case-insensitive or case-sensitive behaviour where the default is not what you want.
hint: One adds a clause, one indexes an expression, one names a collation on the column.

pairs.left: MySQL, where you need case to matter
PostgreSQL, where you need case ignored
SQLite, where you need case ignored

prompt: What is the rule this section ends on?
hint: It is about who decides, rather than which behaviour is correct.

choices.text: Compare text case-insensitively, since users type carelessly
choices.why: Right for an address and wrong for a token or a hash. Neither behaviour is right everywhere.

choices.text: Do not let a default decide what the application cares about
choices.why: If two strings must be one value, say so in the schema; if they must differ, say that.

choices.text: Store text lowercased, and compare the lowered form
choices.why: That destroys a value you may need to show back, and it is wrong for anything case-significant.

choices.text: Use the engine whose default matches your data
choices.why: One database holds addresses and tokens at once, so no single default fits it.

prompt: `SELECT 'MN' || '-330'` returned `1` on MySQL. What did the engine do?
hint: `||` is not concatenation there.

choices.text: It concatenated and then cast the result to a number
choices.why: It never concatenated. `||` is not the concatenation operator on that engine.

choices.text: It read `||` as logical OR, and one side was not zero
choices.why: `'-330'` is truthy, so the OR is true, printed as `1`. No error and no warning in the result.

choices.text: It failed, and the client printed the error code instead
choices.why: It did not fail, which is why this is a trap rather than a lookup.

choices.text: It returned the number of strings it was given
choices.why: There is no such operator; the `1` is a boolean result.

prompt: Which spelling of concatenation works on all four engines?
hint: One of the two is refused, or worse, silently means something else.

choices.why: It concatenates on PostgreSQL and SQLite and is logical OR on MySQL and MariaDB.

choices.text: `CONCAT(a, b)`
choices.why: The portable spelling, and it costs nothing to prefer it.

choices.text: `a + b`
choices.why: That is numeric addition on three of them, and on MySQL it converts the strings to numbers.

choices.text: `CONCAT_WS(a, b)`
choices.why: That exists on MySQL and takes a separator as its first argument, so it does something else.

prompt: A schema is ported from MySQL to PostgreSQL. The tables and the data arrive intact, and a screen that lists a customer's orders becomes noticeably slower. What is the likely cause?
hint: Compare what each engine builds under a foreign key without being asked.

choices.text: PostgreSQL enforces foreign keys and MySQL did not
choices.why: InnoDB enforces them too. The difference is the index, not the constraint.

choices.text: PostgreSQL did not index the foreign key, and MySQL had
choices.why: `SHOW CREATE TABLE` printed `KEY customer_id`; `\d orders` showed only the primary key. The lookup is now a scan.

choices.text: The data types changed, so the join no longer uses an index
choices.why: A plausible worry, and here there was no index to lose on the new side.

choices.text: PostgreSQL needs ANALYZE before it will use any index
choices.why: Statistics matter, and there is no index on that column to be chosen even with perfect statistics.

prompt: A migration runs six `ALTER TABLE` statements inside a transaction and the fourth fails. What is left behind on MySQL?
hint: Ask whether the ROLLBACK had anything to undo.

choices.text: The old schema: the transaction rolled the first three back
choices.why: That is PostgreSQL and SQLite. MySQL commits implicitly around every DDL statement.

choices.text: The new schema, since a failed ALTER is skipped
choices.why: The fourth failed and the ones after it never ran.

choices.text: The first three changes, applied and committed
choices.why: Each ALTER committed as it ran, so the schema is neither the old version nor the new one.

choices.text: The schema is locked until an administrator clears it
choices.why: Nothing is left locked; the damage is a half-applied schema that looks fine.

prompt: Which engine in this lesson has no `INSERT … RETURNING`?
hint: Three of the four printed the new id; one printed a syntax error.

choices.text: MySQL
choices.why: A syntax error. The substitute is `LAST_INSERT_ID()`, which has nothing for a multi-row insert.

choices.text: SQLite
choices.why: It has had it since 3.35 and printed `6`.

choices.text: MariaDB
choices.why: It has had it since 10.5 and printed `6`, which is one of the divergences from MySQL.

choices.text: PostgreSQL
choices.why: It has had it since 8.2, and lesson 11 used it.

prompt: Match each engine to how it spells an auto-numbered primary key.
hint: One is a whole clause, one is a keyword, one is a type that means it by convention.

prompt: `5 / 2` is 2 on PostgreSQL and SQLite and 2.5 on MySQL. To get 2.5 everywhere, multiply one side by ___ first.
hint: One literal, and it turns the expression into decimal arithmetic.

prompt: Why does MariaDB exist?
hint: Look at what happened to MySQL's owner in 2009.

choices.text: MySQL's licence changed, so a GPL version had to be written
choices.why: MySQL's community edition is still GPL. The fork was about who would own the project.

choices.text: Its original authors forked it as Oracle acquired Sun
choices.why: Michael Widenius forked the code in 2009, naming it after his other daughter.

choices.text: Oracle discontinued MySQL and a community picked it up
choices.why: MySQL was never discontinued; Oracle still releases it.

choices.text: A cloud provider needed a version of it that it could resell
choices.why: That is the story of some other forks, and not this one.

prompt: Which of these divergences between MySQL 8 and MariaDB 10.11 showed up in this lesson's own transcripts?
hint: Three things were captured differently from the two engines.

choices.text: The storage engine: InnoDB against MyISAM
choices.why: Both defaulted to InnoDB; the captured SHOW CREATE TABLE says so.

choices.text: The collation: case-sensitive on one and not the other
choices.why: Both defaulted to a case-insensitive collation.

choices.text: Whether `||` concatenates or is read as logical OR
choices.why: It is logical OR on both, which is the inheritance rather than the divergence.

choices.text: ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, RETURNING, and the integer width
choices.why: MariaDB answered the ambiguous GROUP BY, MySQL refused; RETURNING worked on one and not the other; DESCRIBE printed the widths differently.

prompt: An application storing documents in a `JSON` column is moved from MySQL 8 to MariaDB 10.11. The queries all run. What should be measured before calling it done?
hint: The type name is accepted on both. Ask what is underneath it.

choices.text: Whether the documents survived the transfer intact
choices.why: Worth checking on any migration, and it is not the difference between these two.

choices.text: Whether the JSON functions used still exist on the new engine
choices.why: They exist, which is exactly why the queries ran and the problem is invisible.

choices.text: How long extracting a field takes on the new engine
choices.why: MySQL stores it in a binary form parsed once. The code moves and the plan does not.

choices.text: Whether the column still refuses invalid JSON
choices.why: MariaDB adds a CHECK for validity, so that part does carry over.

prompt: A developer wants to connect to a MariaDB server and only has the `mysql` client installed. What happens?
hint: What did the fork inherit besides the SQL?

choices.text: It refuses, because the server identifies itself as MariaDB
choices.why: The server name appears in VERSION() and does not stop the connection.

choices.text: It connects; the wire protocol is shared
choices.why: Same protocol, same client, in both directions, which is why most drivers list one and speak to both.

choices.text: It connects, but DDL is refused over that client
choices.why: There is no such restriction; the protocol does not distinguish statement kinds this way.

choices.text: It connects once the server has a compatibility mode switched on
choices.why: No such mode is needed. The protocol was inherited rather than reimplemented.

prompt: The lesson says the choice between MySQL and MariaDB is usually not a technical decision. What does it say instead?
hint: It names what actually puts people on one of them.

choices.text: That MariaDB is technically ahead and should be preferred
choices.why: It is ahead on some rows and behind on others, and the lesson does not rank them that way.

choices.text: That whichever has released more recently should win, the fork being old
choices.why: Both are actively released; age of the fork decides nothing.

choices.text: That the licence should decide it, since one is commercial
choices.why: The community edition is GPL; the discomfort people name is about ownership rather than a term anybody can point to.

choices.text: That where it is genuinely open, PostgreSQL is the better answer
choices.why: The strictness sections are the argument, and the usual reason to be on either is that you already are.

prompt: What does PostgreSQL's streaming replication not include?
hint: It is the part people assume is there and find out about during an incident.

choices.text: Replicas that serve reads
choices.why: Replicas are read-only and can serve reads; that part is built in.

choices.text: Shipping the write-ahead log to the replica
choices.why: That is precisely what streaming replication is.

choices.text: Replaying the log on the replica
choices.why: The replica replays what it receives; that is how it stays current.

choices.text: Automatic failover when the primary dies
choices.why: Promotion is done by an external tool such as Patroni or repmgr, and finding that out during an outage is expensive.

prompt: A team has a nightly `pg_dump` in object storage and no write-ahead log archive. A bad migration runs at 14:00 and is noticed at 16:00. What can they recover to?
hint: Point-in-time recovery needs something the base backup alone does not carry.

choices.text: Any moment before 14:00, using the dump plus the log
choices.why: There is no log archive; rolling forward is exactly what is missing.

choices.text: 13:59, by replaying the transactions from the running server
choices.why: The running server's history is what the migration changed; the log would have to have been archived.

choices.text: The hour the dump was taken, and nothing after it
choices.why: A base backup restores to when it was taken. Rolling forward needs the WAL kept beside it.

choices.text: Nothing, since a logical dump cannot be restored selectively
choices.why: A dump restores fine. The limit is when it was taken, not what it can do.

prompt: What does the lesson say about a backup nobody has restored?
hint: It is blunt about it.

choices.text: It is a file with a hopeful name
choices.why: Restoring one into a scratch server on a schedule is the only test of a backup there is.

choices.text: It is fine as long as the job reports success
choices.why: A job that wrote a file successfully has not shown that the file can be read back.

choices.text: It is acceptable for a logical dump and not for a physical one
choices.why: The rule does not vary by kind; both need restoring to be believed.

choices.text: It counts once the checksum has been verified
choices.why: A checksum shows the bytes survived, not that the database in them comes back.

prompt: A small team with no database administrator is choosing between PostgreSQL and MySQL, on a cloud whose managed service offers both. On these grounds alone, what does the lesson say decides it?
hint: The question that decides it is about people, and this scenario has removed the usual one.

choices.text: PostgreSQL, because it is stricter and that matters more without a DBA
choices.why: A real argument for PostgreSQL, and it is the strictness sections' argument rather than this section's.

choices.text: MySQL, because it is the easier of the two to operate
choices.why: A managed service is doing the operating in both cases, so ease of operation is not what is left.

choices.text: Neither: both are managed, so the earlier sections decide
choices.why: The managed offering is what usually decides, and here it is a tie, so the earlier sections settle it.

choices.text: Whichever the cloud charges less for that month
choices.why: Price varies and the data outlives the billing decision; it is not the criterion the lesson names.

prompt: Put the steps of a PostgreSQL major-version upgrade in order, as the lesson describes it.
hint: The on-disk format changes between major versions, which is why a restart is not enough.
items: Take a backup and confirm you can restore it
Install the new major version alongside the old one
Run pg_upgrade, with the downtime that implies
Start the new version and check the application against it
trap: A minor version is a restart, and treating a major one the same way is how a cluster ends up two years past its support window.

prompt: Which engine's file format has stayed backward-compatible since 2004, with a stated intention to keep it so until 2050?
hint: It is also the one where upgrading means replacing a library.

choices.text: MariaDB
choices.why: It upgrades in place most of the time, which is not the same promise.

choices.text: PostgreSQL
choices.why: Its on-disk format changes between major versions, which is what pg_upgrade exists for.

choices.text: MySQL
choices.why: It upgrades in place with tooling that fixes the system tables; there is no such format promise.

choices.text: SQLite
choices.why: Which is part of why it can be shipped inside applications nobody will update.

prompt: What does the lesson say most developers do about choosing an engine?
hint: It is the first sentence of the section.

choices.text: They choose once, early, and regret it some years later
choices.why: That assumes a choice was made. Usually there was not one.

choices.text: They choose per project, from a shortlist the team keeps
choices.why: A tidy picture, and it is not how most systems acquire their database.

choices.text: They choose whichever their framework defaults to
choices.why: A framework's default matters for a new project, and most work is on an old one.

choices.text: They do not; they join a company that already has one
choices.why: Which is why the second half of the section is four questions to ask about the engine in front of you.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the lesson accepts for being on MySQL or MariaDB? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of the four is named as a reason that is not one.

choices.text: The team has operated it for years
choices.why: The people you have run a system better than the one they read about, and that counts.

choices.text: The software you are deploying is written for it
choices.why: WordPress and a great deal of PHP software assume it; that settles it.

choices.text: It is faster than the alternatives
choices.why: Named as a reason that is not one: on ordinary workloads the difference is smaller than one missing index.

choices.text: You need Galera or Group Replication
choices.why: A shape neither of the other engines offers, and a real reason.

prompt: You have just been given a login to a database you did not build. Put the four questions in the order the lesson asks them.
hint: The first one decides which answers to the rest are even possible.
items: Which engine is this, and which version
What is sql_mode, if it is MySQL or MariaDB
What collation do the text columns use
Are foreign keys being enforced at all
trap: Reading sql_mode before the version is the common slip: the variable does not exist on PostgreSQL or SQLite, and the version decides half of what the rest of your reading will mean.

prompt: You inherit a SQLite database written by an application that never ran `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`. What should you expect?
hint: The declarations are in the schema. Ask whether anything was enforcing them.

choices.text: The foreign key declarations were rejected at CREATE TABLE time
choices.why: They were accepted and recorded. Enforcement is a separate switch, per connection.

choices.text: Rows pointing at parents that are not there
choices.why: The constraint is in the schema and was never checked, so the data may already violate it.

choices.text: A clean database: SQLite enforces them regardless of the pragma
choices.why: They are off by default, which is the surprise this question is about.

choices.text: The foreign key columns will be NULL where the parent was deleted
choices.why: That would be ON DELETE SET NULL doing its job, which needs the enforcement that was never on.

prompt: What is the sentence this lesson ends on, and what does it mean here?
hint: Lesson 11 made the same point one layer up.

choices.text: Pick the strictest engine you can, because strictness is what correctness means
choices.why: Strictness is an argument for PostgreSQL where the choice is open, and it is not what the lesson closes on.

choices.text: Learn one engine deeply, because the differences are too large to carry
choices.why: The differences turned out to be small and specific, and none of them was about the model.

choices.text: Write portable SQL everywhere, so the engine stops mattering
choices.why: The lesson says to write the portable spelling where it is free and the engine's own where it is not.

choices.text: The tools change and the questions do not: the engine decides what is refused, not what is correct
choices.why: Lessons 1 to 11 are the same subject on all four, which is why they were written without a product name in them.

prompt: For a new SQLite database, the two habits are: declare every table ___, and keep money as an integer number of cents.
hint: One keyword, added after the closing bracket of CREATE TABLE.
